newsitem.title: CANADA: Delayed, smaller Zaire mission gets green light.
newsitem.headline: Delayed, smaller Zaire mission gets green light.

text.p: A Canadian-led international force to assist refugees in eastern Zaire got the official go-ahead on Friday to begin scaled-down operations, a Canadian official said.
"Now the multinational force is formally constituted," Canadian Assistant Deputy Foreign Minister Paul Heinbecker told reporters after chairing a meeting of ambassadors from 14 nations.

More than 20 countries including the United States, France, Britain, Belgium, Senegal and South Africa will contribute to the mission, more likely to comprise 1,000 or 2,000 troops instead of the 10,000 originally planned.

The green light came nearly three weeks after Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien began urging world leaders to rescue what aid agencies then said were more than a million refugees and displaced people in strife-torn eastern Zaire.

Since then about 600,000 refugees have returned to Rwanda. Heinbecker said at least 140,000 more have been identified in Zaire, and Western officials have said there could be hundreds of thousands of others along with displaced Zairians.
Friday's meeting approved a Canadian proposal to set up a multinational military headquarters in Entebbe, Uganda, pursue reconnaissance missions and prepare for possible airdrops.

Ideally, aid would be delivered through truck convoys rather than dropped from the air, Canadian officials said. But the Rwandan government and Tutsi rebels in neighbouring eastern Zaire have been hindering the convoys.
"If the permission is given for the convoys to drive in, they'll go in," Heinbecker said.
"I'm not saying it's a panacea, (that) it's a full answer," Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy told Parliament, when asked about the Canadian plan.
"But I do know that most Canadians ... want this country to continue to provide leadership to mobilise ... the international community to support humanitarian aid," he said.
Canada already has positioned almost 300 people and the United States almost 400 in the area, mostly in Entebbe.
Asked what would change immediately at Entebbe, Heinbecker said: "They were operating nationally. As of now they are operating multinationally."
It would now be up to Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, the force commander, to piece together exactly what the mission would require, and what each country would do.
A top priority would be to intensify reconnaissance in eastern Zaire to identify people in need before any airdrops could be undertaken.
Heinbecker said 40,000 refugees in eastern Zaire appeared to be trudging towards Rwanda, heading from Sake to Goma, the town where most have crossed so far.
A much larger group, believed to be in excess of 100,000 people, was isolated in the mountains, he said.
Axworthy said Canada had consulted with humanitarian agencies before putting the airdrop idea forward.

Zairian Information Minister Boguo Makeli said the Zairian government would not allow overflights for airdrops, but Axworthy said Canada had obtained the full approval of Zairian President Mobutu Sese Seko.

The countries in the "steering group" for the force were Belgium, Britain, Cameroon (for the Organisation of African Unity), Canada, France, Ireland (for the European Union), Italy, Japan, Senegal, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Uganda and the United States.

Senegal has offered 800 troops, Japan is providing money, Italy is sending two or three C-130 Hercules transports. On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry said he was unable to say if more U.S. troops would be committed.
